genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the specialist works with athletes who practise swimming
she begins by watching the athletes launch themselves off the edge
she looks for the movements that squander strength
she spends the second part of the day in a weights room
she teaches beginners to take hold of the load without tensing the upper back
she finishes with a study of the training logs
she ran middle distance before she took up coaching
she says her craft comes from her own physical injuries
she rejects identical plans for everyone
she reckons that suppleness brings more progress than rigid strength
text: The conditioning coach at a swimming club splits her week between three quite separate jobs. Her mornings belong to the poolside, where she watches the swimmers launch themselves off the edge, follows the way the knees fold before the push, and picks out the movements that squander strength for nothing. The second half of the day goes to the weights room; there she corrects the footing and teaches newcomers to take hold of the bar without tensing the upper back. Evenings are for the training logs, which she reads through and annotates with the patience of a copyist. A stocky woman, once a middle-distance runner herself, she says she learnt the craft by listening to her own injuries. She will not hand two athletes the same programme, and she holds to one idea: a supple swimmer improves further than a strong but rigid one.

units: the narrator recounts her visit to an indoor venue given over to climbing
her first impression of the welcome was poor
the lockers for clothes worked badly
she thought about giving up and leaving
an instructor taught her the right way to take hold of the grips
she lost her balance on the way back down and nobody mocked her
the crowd made the place noisy later on
the way the climbers helped one another made her forget the noise
she finds the price fair and the walls well designed
she criticises the changing cubicles and means to come back
text: Right, let me say it plainly: that indoor climbing centre won me over. The welcome struck me as shambolic, the lockers jammed on every second try, and I very nearly walked straight back out. Then an instructor came across and showed me how to take hold of a grip without crushing my fingers, and the session turned. I climbed an easy route, lost my footing on the way back down, and nobody laughed. Later the place filled up, the noise rose with it, and I grumbled inwardly. But the climbers passed advice around without shoving past one another, and the din dissolved into the effort. I came out with my forearms burning and that daft grin of a beginner who has just worked a movement out. Fair price, walls beautifully set, changing cubicles crying out for a rethink. I am going back next week.

units: the writer sends news to a member of her family
a structure that crosses a waterway has been shut for works
that closure made the training circuit unusable
the man in charge moved the sessions to a disused stone workings
the soft ground there forces the lower joints to bend further
pain at the back of the foot has dropped markedly
the grainy ground cushions the impacts better than the hard surface
passers-by saw the group from the road and signed up
the number of members has doubled
the reader is invited to come and try with borrowed kit
text: Dear cousin, you wanted news of the running club, and the news is good, though the reason for it verges on the comic. The footbridge over the canal has been shut for repairs, which chopped our usual loop into two stretches that lead nowhere. Left without a route, the coach moved the sessions to the old stone workings, where the loose ground forces the ankles and knees to bend a great deal further. The effect showed at once: heel pain has all but gone, since the grit swallows the impact that the hard surface used to throw back at us. And because the place sits in plain view of the road, walkers stopped to watch, then signed up, and our numbers have doubled. I am telling you this because you said you wanted to start again. Come along one morning, and we will lend you a pair of shoes.

units: the text deals with a joint of the upper arm that has been left idle
idleness brings on stiffening, according to the specialists in rehabilitation
the discomfort felt puts the sufferer off moving even more
a violent strain is unwise because it wakes the pain again
the answer put forward is a very small range of movement, repeated
the first exercise lets the limb swing freely
a very light weight is then brought in, such as an empty container
if the discomfort returns, one must go back to an earlier stage
the improvement does not come at a steady rate
whoever hurries the process fails again and again
text: What becomes of a shoulder that stops being used? It seizes up, say the specialists in rehabilitation, and the discomfort that follows puts the sufferer off moving it any further. The circle closes on itself. Should the joint be forced, then? No: a violent pull wakes the pain and drives the shoulder to guard itself all the harder. What remains? A tiny range of movement, repeated without haste, kept up over weeks. You begin by letting the arm hang and swing of its own accord, like a pendulum that nothing is pushing. Then comes a laughably light weight, an empty bottle, and later something barely heavier. And if the ache creeps back? You drop down a stage, without making a drama of it, for progress here rarely runs in a straight line. Whoever accepts that slowness ends up with a working shoulder; whoever hurries replays the same failure without end.

units: a specialist carer describes two techniques for coming back to the ground
the first technique keeps the lower limbs straight
that first option sends the shock right up to the top of the legs
the middle joint of the leg then carries the load
the second technique folds the hips and the knees at the moment of contact
the muscles at the front of the leg then cushion like a spring
the patient finds the second option harder work
the carer grants that tiredness but prefers it to damage of the joint tissue
a noisy return to the ground points to badly controlled cushioning
a quiet return to the ground reveals a movement under control
text: The physiotherapist was setting out for his patient the two ways a body has of meeting the ground at the end of a jump. The first, he said, is to land with the legs straight: nothing breaks the shock, it runs right up to the top of the legs, and the knee takes very nearly all of it. The second asks you to fold the hips and the knees the instant your feet touch, so that the muscles at the front of the thigh slow the drop as a spring would. The patient objected that the second way felt a good deal harder than the first. The therapist granted him that readily, then added that tired muscles cost far less than the wearing away of cartilage. He closed on a distinction that beginners tend to muddle: a loud landing is one that happened to you, whereas a quiet landing is one you steered yourself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the physical activities of the distant past are sorted into categories by specialists
the sorting rests on the end that was pursued
the first category sets two wrestlers against each other on a cramped surface
such contests turn up in almost every society that settled for good
the second category gathers the trials of speed over lengths of every sort
those trials put the honour of the community at stake
the third category has to do with sending an object far off
the vocabulary of those movements survives in the disciplines of today
the fourth category brings together the ball games with their local rules
such practices wove together exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels
text: The movement games of the distant past sort into separate families, which researchers tell apart by the end each one served. First come the trials of strength, where two wrestlers take hold of each other and try to unbalance an opponent on a cramped patch of ground; they turn up almost everywhere that people settled for good. Then come the races, run over lengths of every sort, often barefoot, with the standing of a whole village riding on the outcome. A third family gathers the throws, where a stone, a shaft or a disc is sent as far as the arm allows, and whose movements have handed their vocabulary down to the sports we watch today. A fourth brings together the ball games, whose rules shifted from one valley to the next. These practices, historians add, wove exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels into a single thing.

units: the contraction of a muscle follows a strictly ordered sequence
the thinking organ fires an electrical pulse as soon as an intention appears
that pulse travels along a nerve conductor
a chemical is released at the point of contact with the fibre
very fine elements slide past one another and shorten the fibre
the attaching cord then pulls on the piece of bone
the limb moves because of that pull
the filaments let go once the movement is finished
the whole process takes a very short span of time
the breathing quickens when the fibres run short of fuel
text: A muscle that contracts does so through a run of steps whose order never varies. Everything starts in the brain, which fires off an electrical pulse the moment an intention to move takes shape. The pulse runs down a nerve, reaches the point where the nerve meets the fibre, and releases a chemical there. The fibre answers at once: minute filaments slide past one another and the whole of it shortens. The tendon, hauled on from within, drags the bone it is fixed to, and the limb swings into motion. As soon as the movement is over, the filaments let go and the fibre stretches out again. The whole of that sequence lasts no more than a fraction of a second. When it runs on and on, the runner begins to gasp, because the fibres are calling for a fuel that the breath can barely supply.

units: the narrator was coming home from an evening swim
he took a narrow path that runs past a storage building
the recent rain had made the slope slippery
he thought he would gain time going down rather than round the slope
his foot slid on a root he could not see
he fell and landed in the mud
his open bag let his belongings spill out
he had to crawl along the ground to gather his things one by one
a passer-by handed him a towel without a word
he now takes the tarmac route
text: Coming home from the swimming pool the other evening, I had the bright idea of cutting along the narrow path that skirts the warehouse. It had rained, the slope was greasy, and I told myself I would get down it faster than round it. So I let my legs go, and my left foot slid on a root I never saw. I stumbled, flailed my arms like a puppet on strings, and ended up sitting in the mud with my bag hanging open. Out of that open bag my things rolled off in every direction, and I had to crawl about on the ground to gather them up one at a time. A walker handed me my towel without a word, looking terribly busy not laughing. Home I went, soaked through, caked in drying mud and thoroughly put out. Since then I take the tarmac road round, and I put rather less pride into my short cuts.

units: going back to running after an ankle injury worries ordinary athletes
a joint that has been poorly retrained gives way at the first step that lands askew
coaches put forward an approach in four stages
the first stage is to hold yourself up on the injured leg
that posture lasts about thirty calm breathing cycles
the second stage repeats the exercise with the eyes closed
closing the eyes removes the visual cues and calls on the receptors of the joint
the third stage brings in short hops on the spot with a turn of the hips
the last stage offers gentle strides that lengthen little by little
any sharp pain means stopping and going back to the stage before
text: Going back to running after a sprain unnerves most weekend athletes, and the worry is well founded: an ankle that has not been properly retrained gives way the first time a step lands askew. The routine that coaches recommend comes in four stages. Start by holding yourself up on the injured foot, arms loose at your sides, for about thirty calm breaths. Move on to the same posture with your eyelids shut, which strips away every visual cue and forces the receptors inside the joint to wake up. Then bring in short hops on the spot, turning the hips as you land and keeping the heel from drifting outwards. Finish with slow strides on even ground, adding a little distance from one session to the next. Stop everything the moment a sharp pain shows itself, and pick up again at the stage before, the following day.

units: two groups of runners share the same sports ground at the end of the day
the training goes on as night draws in
the sprinters have a heavy build and thick legs
they put out a violent effort over a short run of strides
they then pull up dead, short of breath
the long-distance runners are leaner and go round without a break
their breathing keeps to a steady rhythm
the speed specialists get their wind back by walking
a woman in charge of the training watches both camps
she notes that one lot stare at the timing device and the other lot at the sky
text: The track smells of wet dust, and as the light goes two groups are sharing it. On one side the sprinters: blocky frames, heavy thighs, waiting quite still, then detonating over a bare thirty strides before pulling up dead, gasping, hands on hips. On the other the distance runners, leaner and looser, going round and round without a break, chests calm, breathing ticking over like a metronome. The first lot spend the lot in one brief flare, then walk it off along the fence to get their wind back. The second spare every movement and hardly ever stop. A coach watches both camps from the finish line and remarks that the sprinters stare at the stopwatch while the distance runners stare at the sky. Their event, she says, shows plainly in the way that each of them carries fatigue.
